verses.text: Shephatiah the son of Mattan, and Gedaliah the son of Pashhur, and Jucal the son of Shelemiah, and Pashhur the son of Malchijah, heard the words that Jeremiah spoke to all the people, saying,

“Yahweh says, ‘He who remains in this city shall die by the sword, by the famine, and by the pestilence; but he who goes out to the Chaldeans shall live, and his life shall be to him for a prey, and he shall live.’
Yahweh says, ‘This city will surely be given into the hand of the army of the king of Babylon, and he will take it.’”

Then the princes said to the king, “Please let this man be put to death; because he weakens the hands of the men of war who remain in this city, and the hands of all the people, in speaking such words to them: for this man doesn’t seek the welfare of this people, but harm.”
Zedekiah the king said, “Behold, he is in your hand; for the king can’t do anything to oppose you.”

Then took they Jeremiah, and cast him into the dungeon of Malchijah the king’s son, that was in the court of the guard. They let down Jeremiah with cords. In the dungeon there was no water, but mire; and Jeremiah sank in the mire.
Now when Ebedmelech the Ethiopian, a eunuch, who was in the king’s house, heard that they had put Jeremiah in the dungeon (the king was then sitting in the gate of Benjamin),
Ebedmelech went out of the king’s house, and spoke to the king, saying,

“My lord the king, these men have done evil in all that they have done to Jeremiah the prophet, whom they have cast into the dungeon. He is likely to die in the place where he is, because of the famine; for there is no more bread in the city.”
Then the king commanded Ebedmelech the Ethiopian, saying, “Take from here thirty men with you, and take up Jeremiah the prophet out of the dungeon, before he dies.”
So Ebedmelech took the men with him, and went into the house of the king under the treasury, and took there rags and worn-out garments, and let them down by cords into the dungeon to Jeremiah.
Ebedmelech the Ethiopian said to Jeremiah, “Now put these rags and worn-out garments under your armpits under the cords.” Jeremiah did so.
So they drew up Jeremiah with the cords, and took him up out of the dungeon; and Jeremiah remained in the court of the guard.
Then Zedekiah the king sent, and took Jeremiah the prophet to himself into the third entry that is in Yahweh’s house. Then the king said to Jeremiah, “I will ask you something. Hide nothing from me.”
Then Jeremiah said to Zedekiah, “If I declare it to you, will you not surely put me to death? If I give you counsel, you will not listen to me.”
So Zedekiah the king swore secretly to Jeremiah, saying, “As Yahweh lives, who made us this soul, I will not put you to death, neither will I give you into the hand of these men who seek your life.”

Then Jeremiah said to Zedekiah, “Yahweh, the God of Armies, the God of Israel, says: ‘If you will go out to the king of Babylon’s princes, then your soul will live, and this city will not be burned with fire. You will live, along with your house.
But if you will not go out to the king of Babylon’s princes, then this city will be given into the hand of the Chaldeans, and they will burn it with fire, and you won’t escape out of their hand.’”
Zedekiah the king said to Jeremiah, “I am afraid of the Jews who have defected to the Chaldeans, lest they deliver me into their hand, and they mock me.”
But Jeremiah said, “They won’t deliver you. Obey, I beg you, Yahweh’s voice, in that which I speak to you; so it will be well with you, and your soul shall live.
But if you refuse to go out, this is the word that Yahweh has shown me:

‘Behold, all the women who are left in the king of Judah’s house will be brought out to the king of Babylon’s princes, and those women will say, “Your familiar friends have turned on you, and have prevailed over you. Your feet are sunk in the mire, they have turned away from you.”

They will bring out all your wives and your children to the Chaldeans. You won’t escape out of their hand, but will be taken by the hand of the king of Babylon. You will cause this city to be burned with fire.’”
Then Zedekiah said to Jeremiah, “Let no man know of these words, and you won’t die.

But if the princes hear that I have talked with you, and they come to you, and tell you, ‘Declare to us now what you have said to the king; don’t hide it from us, and we will not put you to death; also what the king said to you;’
then you shall tell them, ‘I presented my supplication before the king, that he would not cause me to return to Jonathan’s house, to die there.’”
Then came all the princes to Jeremiah, and asked him; and he told them according to all these words that the king had commanded. So they stopped speaking with him; for the matter was not perceived.
So Jeremiah stayed in the court of the guard until the day that Jerusalem was taken.

footnotes.content: Four princes gather around the king—Shephatiah, Gedaliah, Jucal, Pashhur—to repeat what Jeremiah spoke. These men are powerful at court, yet their ears are closed. Sometimes the most dangerous listeners are those with the power to choose: they hear, but turn their face away.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jeremiah tells the city: stay and you die; surrender and you live. This is the hard word the Lord gave him—not comfort, but truth. In a siege, surrender seems like defeat, yet it's the door to life. The Lord often asks us to lay down what we think we must grip.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Babylon will take the city—Jeremiah says it with certainty because the Lord has already spoken it. When we know what the Lord has said, we can stand firm even when everything around us trembles. His word doesn't change because we wish it would.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The princes accuse Jeremiah of weakening the soldiers' resolve—yet he speaks only what God gave him. Truth-telling is often called disloyalty by those who want comforting lies instead. To love a people well sometimes means speaking hard words that feel like betrayal.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Zedekiah says the prophet is in their hands—the king abdicates. A ruler who cannot rule, who hides behind princes instead of bearing his own weight: this is a man already broken by fear. Jesus later stood before Pilate; Pilate stood before the crowd. Fear often turns leaders inside-out.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They lower Jeremiah into the dungeon's mire on cords—no water, only mud. The court of the guard becomes his tomb. But the Lord sees men in darkness; He never forgets a faithful voice, even when the world buries it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Ebedmelech the Ethiopian, a foreigner and a eunuch—low in status, yet the Lord places compassion in his heart. He hears of Jeremiah's plight while the king sits in judgment at the gate, blind to it. The Lord often acts through the ones the world overlooks.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Ebedmelech goes out of the king's house and speaks to the king directly. No permission asked, no politicking—he simply acts in mercy. There is a boldness that comes from knowing something matters more than station or fear.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Ebedmelech calls it evil—what the princes did to God's prophet is wrong, and he says so plainly. The famine and the dungeon spell death; Ebedmelech sees this and will not let it pass. Such courage often comes from the quiet, faithful heart.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The king commands: take thirty men and pull the prophet out before he dies. One word from a fearful king, yet it comes—the Lord's hand moves through it. Sometimes deliverance arrives suddenly, in the space between despair and the grave.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Ebedmelech gathers rags and worn garments from the treasury—not fine cloth, but what will protect. Rescue often looks humble and rough. The Lord's mercy doesn't always come dressed in royal silks; sometimes it arrives in old cloth and strong hands.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Ebedmelech tells Jeremiah to put the rags under his arms—a small kindness amid crisis. The prophet does it without question. When you're in the mire, you trust the hands reaching down, and you obey. Faith in rescue means letting someone help.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They draw him up with cords and he remains in the court of the guard. From the mire to safety—not freedom yet, but life preserved. The Lord raises the faithful through unlikely servants; Jeremiah lives another day because a foreign eunuch acted in mercy.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Zedekiah summons Jeremiah to the third entry of the temple—a secret meeting. Even as the princes imprison the prophet, the king cannot let him go. A man bound to fear cannot find freedom, yet he seeks counsel from the very voice that terrifies him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jeremiah asks: if I speak, will you kill me? If I give counsel, will you listen? The prophet has learned the king's heart: Zedekiah wants comfort, not truth. It is a hard thing to speak to a man who asks for your honesty but plans to punish it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Zedekiah swears by the living God: I will not kill you, nor hand you over. A secret oath, whispered in the temple's darkness. Yet an oath made in fear is often fragile—the king swears what he wishes were true of himself, not what his fear will allow him to keep.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jeremiah speaks: go out to Babylon's princes, and you live—you and your house. It is the only way. This is not Jeremiah's word; it is the Lord's, spoken through the prophet's mouth. To obey God sometimes means to lay down the last thing we hold.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: If you refuse, Jerusalem burns and you will not escape. The choice stands clear: surrender or destruction. The Lord offers life through humbling; Zedekiah sees the choice and knows he will not take it. His fear chooses death for himself and his city.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Zedekiah fears the Jews who have already defected—he fears being mocked, abandoned by his own. Pride and fear are cruel masters; they make a man choose ruin over humility. When we fear man's judgment more than God's will, we lose both.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They won't deliver you, Jeremiah says—obey the Lord's voice through me, and it will be well. The prophet offers the path to life one more time. He pleads with the king to hear, knowing already that Zedekiah's ear is closed by the weight of fear.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: But if you refuse, this is the word the Lord shows me: Jeremiah does not turn away. He will speak the hard word because the Lord has shown it to him, because Zedekiah asked and deserves to hear. Faithfulness means speaking even when you know the hearer will not listen.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The women of the palace will be brought out, mocking you—your friends have turned against you, your feet sink in the mire. The word comes to the man already acquainted with betrayal. There is a pattern: those who reject God's mercy often find themselves sinking into the very trap they feared.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Your wives and children will be taken; you won't escape; the city burns. The prophecy is complete and terrible. Jeremiah has spoken it now, given Zedekiah the last word of the Lord, and the king has rejected it. Mercy offered and refused is a threshold no one crosses unscathed.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Zedekiah tells Jeremiah: tell no one we spoke, and you won't die. The king's plea is a bargain: keep silence and live. But secrets wrung from fear are never quite kept, and the prophet's life hangs on the king's whim—a thin thread indeed.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: If the princes find out you spoke with me, they'll demand to know what I said. They'll say, tell us what the king commanded, or we'll kill you. The king lays bare the trap: Jeremiah is caught between the princes and the king, between silence and death.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Tell them you asked not to be sent back to Jonathan's house to die—a half-truth that saves. Zedekiah coaches the prophet in deception, and Jeremiah does as he is told. Even the faithful sometimes must navigate the crooked ways of fearful power.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: All the princes come and ask; Jeremiah tells them the cover story; they stop pressing and the matter goes no further. The lie holds. The Lord's prophet lives another day by speaking a half-truth. God does not always demand martyrdom; sometimes He preserves His word for a harder road ahead.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jeremiah stayed in the court of the guard until Jerusalem fell. Readers today hear an echo in this: the Lord's faithful servants often survive their cities' ruin. Jesus walked through the Temple's judgment alone; so too does the prophet endure. Looking back from 2026-10, I see how the Lord keeps His witnesses alive for reasons we only grasp later.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
